title.title: A counterexample to Sidorenko's conjecture
title.subtitle: Claim: a bipartite pattern with 35 vertices and 66 edges is rarer in some graph than in a random one

plain: Sidorenko: for two-sided patterns, a random network has the fewest copies. A 66-edge pattern says otherwise

beats.text: Sidorenko: at edge density $p$, random graphs minimise copies of every bipartite $H$
The claim: this 66-edge pattern is rarer in some host than in a random graph

steps: Pick a pattern where every covered pair of points lies in two triples
Build a host from matrices over a finite field: copies dip
Sample a finite graph that keeps the dip

achievement.label: Sidorenko's conjecture (1993) and the forcing conjecture
statement: t(H,G) \ge p(G)^{e(H)} \text{ for every bipartite } H
achievement.context: Proved for trees, even cycles, hypercubes and more; computer searches in 2025 found nothing
achievement.note: The host $G$ is sampled, not explicit; the forcing part is not in Lean

verify.detail: Strict $t(H,G) < p^{66}$ with the 22 triples hard-coded. The forcing part is out of scope
verify.ourCheck: We read the Lean statement; we did not build it

voice.text: Sidorenko said random graphs hold the fewest copies of any two-sided pattern.
A finite-field construction makes this pattern rarer, and a sampled graph keeps it rare.
Claimed: a host with fewer copies than random.

sources.quote: 22 triples on 13 points, every one of the 33 covered point pairs in exactly two triples
H is connected and bipartite with 35 vertices and 66 edges
Conjectured by Sidorenko (1991/1993, Graphs and Combinatorics 9
The Lean statement hard-codes the 22 triples and asserts strict inequality against `edgeDensity ^ 66`
The forcing-conjecture consequence is explicitly out of scope per lean/docs/161.md
